sweep_summary: Krio (krio1253) is coded 'tonal' on Finney 2013 (APiCS survey 15) with Yakpo 2021 as secondary. this search of works with stress in the title's only title hit is Berry 1970, 'A Note on the Prosodic Structure of Krio', IJAL 36(4):266-267 (doi 10.1086/465120), already in our per-language bibliography. It is closed access everywhere (Crossref, Unpaywall, OpenAlex, Semantic Scholar all report closed/no repository copy; publisher landing and PDF could not be reached by automated download; archive.org holds only the 1970 vol. 36 table of contents, which lists the note; Second-hand, the held open sources agree on its content: Nylander 1984 (SAL 15(2):164 n.4-5) treats Berry 1970b as the companion to Berry 1970a 'A note on Krio tones', the Mona 1968 paper that ended the Strevens 'stress and intonation' view, and Yakpo 2021 sec. 3.1 cites Berry 1970 for Krio's equipollent H/L tone system with a culminative obligatory H on English-derived words. Nothing read contradicts the catalog; the best first-hand statement read is Nylander 1984 pp. 164-165 (already held by the project from the 9/16 check), which confirms 'tonal' and does not supersede Finney 2013. Acquisition priority for Berry 1970b: medium; the fuller primaries (Berry 1970a African Language Studies 11:48-59; Finney 2004 doi 10.1075/cll.27.11fin; Finney 2025 ch. 5 doi 10.1515/9783110784541-005) remain the higher-value targets. Records with and updated.

new_statements.quote: In 1959, Jack Berry identified Krio as a tone language. [...] Strevens [1965:116] described Krio as having "a system of stress and intonation of the same nature as that of Received Pronunciation." [...] It was only in 1968, at the Mona Conference on Pidgins and Creoles, that it was generally agreed that Krio is a tone language. The consensus followed the presentation of another paper by Berry. Hymes [1971:285] observes: The generally accepted view (most recently stated by Strevens) that an original tonal system has been replaced in Krio by a sentence-stress and intonation system is now clearly seen to be untenable.
new_statements.citation: Nylander, Dudley K. 1984. The relation between the middle tone and "Empty Category Principle" violations in Krio. Studies in African Linguistics 15(2): 163-175.
new_statements.locator: sec. 1 'Studies on Krio Tones', pp. 164-165 with notes 4-5
new_statements.reading: A first-hand tonal analysis (open access, held by the project since the 2026-09-16 check and already recorded in the store; re-read in this search of works with stress in the title, scanned 'clesrly' normalized to 'clearly'). Nylander states that Krio's word prosody is tonal (two tones H and L in polysyllables; mid tone only a phonetic variant of H in monosyllables), gives tonal minimal pairs (bàbá/bábà, kòkó/kókó, wòwó/wówò, sòsó/sósó), and records that the Strevens 1965 'stress and intonation' view was abandoned in 1968 after Berry's Mona paper (published as Berry 1970a, with the works with stress in the title Berry 1970b as 'see also'). Note 5 lists Coker 1977, Coomber 1969, Fyle & Jones 1980, Johnson 1974 and Nylander 1979/1981b/1983b as confirming the tonal status. This confirms the catalog's 'tonal' coding; it does not supersede Finney 2013 (the language's principal describer, with the APiCS minimal-pair table) as the deciding source, and it says nothing about a stress rule because it holds there is none.
new_statements.check: confirmed by a second reader, with minor differences

audit.reasoning: Quote check: both deciding passages (Finney 2013 APiCS sec. 4 Table 3 and sec. 9.2; Yakpo 2021 secs. 3.1, 3.5) are present verbatim in the text we hold strips at the stated locators. Deciding source: a 2013 survey sketch by the principal describer of Krio phonology, with the explicit 'tone language without stress' wording taken from a 2021 secondary areal article; grade open-text is honest. Best-available check: Glottolog's 48-row list and CrossRef show better primaries we do not hold -- Finney 2025 De Gruyter Mouton monograph ch. 5 (pp. 66-102; probed, not open), Finney 2004 Benjamins tone-assignment paper (paywalled), Fyle & Jones 1980 OUP dictionary and Nylander 1983 thesis (print only), Berry 1970a/b (print/JSTOR). No JIPA Illustration exists (Cambridge JIPA search: 0 results)

sources.quote: p.163 abstract: 'An examination of monosyllabic words in Krio reveals the existence of three distinct tones: high, mid and low. In words of more than one syllable, however, only two tones are attested: high and low.
